newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Administrator, daughter beheaded in Central Africa.
newsitem.headline: Administrator, daughter beheaded in Central Africa.

text.p: A regional administrator and his young daughter were beheaded in tribal bloodletting that has followed a month-long army mutiny in Central African Republic, witnesses said on Saturday.

Despite the arrival of a regional mediator to try and resolve the crisis, fear gripped the capital Bangui and hundreds of people resumed an exodus to the provinces. Travellers reported mounting ethnic feuding in the interior.
Witnesses said Simon Goner, prefect of Basse-Kotto district, and his daughter were abducted on Monday by unknown people and their headless bodies were later found in a bush.
Their killing was widely believed to be a tribal revenge for the murder in the capital Bangui last week of former interior minister Christophe Grelombe and his son.
Witnesses said the two men, who are from the Yakoma tribe to which most of the mutineers belong, had been abducted from their Bangui home by soldiers loyal to President Ange-Felix Patasse.
Goner is a relation of Patasse, and the Mobaye locality in Basse-Koto district where he and his daughter were killed is in Yakoma heartland, about 700 km (435 miles) east of Bangui.
The district is in one of the most inaccessible parts of the country and news of the killings reached Bangui only on Friday.

Reports of the beheadings spread in the capital as former Malian military ruler General Amadou Toumani Toure began talks there, following up regional mediation initiated last week by the presidents of Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon and Mali.

State radio said Toure met Patasse on Friday night shortly after arriving at the head of a delegation of experts from the four countries whose leaders negotaited a 15-day truce between mutineers and government troops just over a week ago.

The radio said Toure on Saturday met other political leaders and the ambassador of former colonial ruler France, whose troops kept Patasse in power during an earlier mutiny in May. The French still protect Patasse and other key locations.
The radio gave no details of either meetings.

The mutineers hardened their original pay demands into a political campaign to unseat Patasse, who won elections in 1993. The mutiny has turned into a bloody feud between Patasse's northern Baya tribe and southern Yakomas who dominate the army.
State radio also said a special French envoy, General Jeannot Lacaze, arrived in Bangui on Friday and urged Toure to seek a prolongation of the ceasefire to January.
State radio quoted Lacaze as saying Patasse could not resign, adding that his ouster was demanded by "extremists among the mutineers".

French troops based in the country under bilateral accords used helicopter gunships to quell the May mutiny. Soldiers revolted earlier in April over pay grievances that carried over into the latest unrest.
The French have maintained a low profile this time, restricting their role to protection of key locations.
